notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest substring of three identical digits, or an empty string if none exists.
Idea: Scan each length-three window; keep the matching triple with the greatest digit.
Technique and why it applies: Checking every length-three window finds the largest triple without numeric conversion.
Invariant: The saved triple is the largest qualifying window scanned so far.
Edge cases: Overlapping windows count; if none qualifies return empty string.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Checking every length-three window finds the largest triple without numeric conversion.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count nodes whose value equals the integer average of all values in that node’s subtree.
Idea: Postorder DFS returns subtree sum and node count, incrementing the answer when integer average equals the node value.
Technique and why it applies: Postorder aggregates make each subtree average available after its children are processed.
Invariant: Each recursive result summarizes the complete subtree rooted at that node.
Edge cases: A leaf averages to itself; null children contribute zero sum and count; integer division is required.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space.
complexity_reason: Postorder aggregates make each subtree average available after its children are processed.

notes:
Task and constraints: Keep the first word and remove each word that is an anagram of the immediately previous kept word.
Idea: Sort each word's characters into a signature and keep the word only if its signature differs from the previous input word.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted signatures identify anagrams, and adjacent comparison enforces the stated removal rule.
Invariant: The previous signature belongs to the immediately preceding word, so only adjacent anagrams are removed.
Edge cases: Keep the first word; nonconsecutive anagrams may both remain; preserve original order.
Complexity: O(n k log k) time and O(nk) signature/output space for n words of length up to k.
complexity_reason: Sorted signatures identify anagrams, and adjacent comparison enforces the stated removal rule.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the integer percentage of characters in s that equal letter.
Idea: Count occurrences of `letter`, multiply by 100, and divide by string length using integer division.
Technique and why it applies: Counting target characters and integer division computes the required whole-number percentage.
Invariant: The numerator is the target-letter count, and integer division floors the percentage.
Edge cases: No occurrences returns zero; the input string is nonempty.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Counting target characters and integer division computes the required whole-number percentage.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if each digit d in num occurs exactly num[d] times in the string.
Idea: Count digits in a ten-slot array, then verify each position i equals the frequency of digit i.
Technique and why it applies: A frequency table directly checks each digit's required occurrence count.
Invariant: The frequency array is complete before positional checks begin.
Edge cases: Digits are decimal; the bounded digit alphabet needs only ten counters.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: A frequency table directly checks each digit's required occurrence count.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum number of copies of target that can be formed from s.
Idea: Count letters in s and target, then minimize `have[c] // need[c]` over target letters.
Technique and why it applies: The smallest supply-to-demand ratio limits the number of complete target copies.
Invariant: Each quotient bounds how many copies are possible for that required character.
Edge cases: Repeated target letters require their full multiplicity; target is nonempty; letters are lowercase.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(1) alphabet space.
complexity_reason: The smallest supply-to-demand ratio limits the number of complete target copies.

notes:
Task and constraints: Apply the percentage discount to valid price tokens and format them to two decimal places.
Idea: Split the sentence preserving spaces; transform only tokens beginning with `$` whose remaining characters are all digits, and format the discounted amount to two decimals.
Technique and why it applies: Token validation avoids altering ordinary text while correctly formatting valid prices.
Invariant: Only validated numeric price tokens change; all other tokens remain unchanged.
Edge cases: A bare dollar sign or a token with nondigits is not a price; preserve original spaces and use stable decimal formatting.
Complexity: O(L) time and O(L) output space for sentence length L.
complexity_reason: Token validation avoids altering ordinary text while correctly formatting valid prices.

notes:
Task and constraints: Repeatedly replace each adjacent pair with min, max, min, max until one value remains.
Idea: Repeatedly replace pairs with min for even pair index and max for odd pair index until one value remains.
Technique and why it applies: Pair-index parity selects the alternating minimum and maximum operation each round.
Invariant: Each round forms the next sequence in order and halves its length.
Edge cases: Input length is a power of two; final sequence has one value.
Complexity: O(n) total time; O(n) Python copy space or O(1) extra Java space.
complexity_reason: Pair-index parity selects the alternating minimum and maximum operation each round.

notes:
Task and constraints: Calculate the total tax paid on income using progressive tax brackets.
Idea: For each bracket, tax only the slice from the prior upper bound to the smaller of income and this bound; stop when income is covered.
Technique and why it applies: Marginal slices avoid taxing earlier income again at a higher rate.
Invariant: The accumulator includes each taxable income slice once, and prev marks the next slice's start.
Edge cases: Income in the first bracket starts at zero; rates are percentages; stop after the bracket containing income.
Complexity: O(b) time and O(1) auxiliary space for b brackets.
complexity_reason: Marginal slices avoid taxing earlier income again at a higher rate.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the greatest English letter that appears in both uppercase and lowercase, or an empty string.
Idea: Record characters, then scan uppercase letters from Z down to A and return the first with its lowercase form present.
Technique and why it applies: Scanning from Z downward returns the greatest letter represented in both cases.
Invariant: Descending search ensures the first match is the greatest valid letter.
Edge cases: Return empty string if no letter has both cases; membership is case-sensitive.
Complexity: O(n+26) time and O(1) alphabet space.
complexity_reason: Scanning from Z downward returns the greatest letter represented in both cases.
